base_prompt: How does a map application balance storing map information on the device with downloading information during use? A response of around 160 words is enough.
text: A map application usually combines on-device storage with on-demand downloads to provide fast, reliable navigation without requiring unlimited phone storage. It keeps essential data locally, such as the app software, saved locations, recent searches, road networks for downloaded regions, and sometimes basic world maps. This allows users to view previously downloaded areas, calculate routes, and receive GPS-based position updates even with poor or no connection. More detailed or frequently changing information is downloaded as needed. Examples include satellite imagery, street-level photos, live traffic speeds, road closures, transit timetables, business hours, reviews, and newly added places. Map data is commonly divided into small geographic tiles, so the app fetches only the area and zoom level currently being viewed rather than an entire country. It may also cache recently used tiles temporarily to reduce repeated downloads. Users can often choose offline regions and storage limits, while the app periodically updates saved maps over Wi-Fi to balance freshness, data use, battery life, and available device space.
